text: It's eleven at night. Tomorrow is the big meeting... or the test results... or the conversation you've been dreading. And you're lying there, running it. What if they ask about the numbers? What if it's bad news? What if I freeze?
It's exhausting. But it also feels... responsible. Like you're working on it. Like if you stopped, something bad would slip through.
Here's the strange part. In one study, people tracked their worries for a month... and about nine out of ten never came true. So why does worry still feel so useful?

It isn't because you're bad at thinking. Psychologists have found that worry really does do something for you. Just... not the thing you think. By the end, you'll know what it's actually doing, and three things that help.
In the early nineteen eighties, a psychologist at Penn State named Thomas Borkovec started studying people who worried a lot. And his team gave worry a definition that is still used today.

Worry, they wrote, is a chain of thoughts and images... loaded with negative feeling... and relatively hard to control. It's an attempt to solve a problem in your head. A problem whose outcome is uncertain... and might be bad.

Notice the key phrase. An attempt to solve a problem. That's why worry feels like work. It runs on the same machinery as planning. You scan the future, you spot the dangers, you rehearse what you'd say.
But there's a difference. Planning ends. You find the next step, you take it, and the thought lets go. Worry doesn't end. It reaches the last what if... and loops back to the first one.

Researchers found a clue about why. When people describe the problems they worry about, their descriptions tend to be vaguer and more abstract than when they describe problems they don't worry about. What if it all goes wrong? Instead of... what exactly would I do on Tuesday?

That idea is called the reduced concreteness theory, from Joachim Stoeber and Borkovec. It isn't settled. Some later studies found worry is more concrete than the theory predicts. But it fits what many people feel. A vague problem has no first step. So the mind keeps circling.
So if worry so rarely solves anything... why do we keep doing it? Borkovec decided to ask the worriers themselves.

In a study published in nineteen ninety-five, Borkovec and Lizabeth Roemer gave college students who worried a lot a list of reasons people give for worrying... and asked them to rate how typical each one was for them.
The reasons will probably sound familiar. Worry motivates me to get things done. Worry helps me prepare for the worst. Worry helps me avoid bad outcomes, or prevent them.
And one that's a little more magical. Worrying about something makes it less likely to happen. As if the worry itself were a kind of protection.

There was one more. Worry distracts me from more emotional things. And the students whose worry was strong enough to meet the criteria for generalized anxiety disorder... stood out on that one. They rated it higher than the other groups did. Keep that one in mind. It comes back.
Now here's where it gets tricky. Most of the time, the bad thing doesn't happen. So you worried... and then nothing happened. And your brain draws a conclusion. The worry worked.

It's like a rain dance in a place where it rains anyway. Every time the rain comes, the dance gets the credit. Researchers call this a superstitious kind of avoidance. The relief you feel when the feared thing doesn't happen rewards the worrying... so you do it again next time.
But how often does the feared thing really not happen? A few years ago, someone finally counted.

In a study published in twenty twenty, Lucas LaFreniere and Michelle Newman, also at Penn State, worked with twenty-nine students with generalized anxiety disorder... a pattern where worry is constant and hard to switch off.
For ten days, they were prompted four times a day to write down what they were worrying about... and what they predicted would happen. Then, for thirty days, they checked. Did it come true?
About ninety-one percent of the worries did not come true. The most common result for a single person was one hundred percent. For seven of them... not one worry came true.
And even among the worries that did come true, about three in ten turned out better than the person had expected.
Before we lean on that number too hard, the honest caveats. It was a small study. Mostly young, white, female students. And it only tracked worries that could be checked within a month.
But it shows the gap. The worry felt like a forecast. It was mostly a false alarm. And the students whose worries came true the least... improved the most during the treatment.
Which raises a bigger question. If worry predicts so badly, maybe predicting isn't its real job. Maybe worry is doing something else.
Back to Borkovec. In nineteen ninety, he and a colleague, Shao Hu, ran an experiment with people who were afraid of public speaking.

Before the test, each person spent a short time in one of three states. Some relaxed. Some thought about neutral things. And some worried. Then they imagined giving a speech, again and again, while their heart rate was measured.
You'd expect the worriers to react the most. They didn't. Their heart rate jumped the least when the speech scene came. But... they reported more fear than the neutral group, not less.

Borkovec's explanation. Worry is mostly words. It's talking to yourself about danger, not picturing it. And that inner talk seems to mute the body's alarm. Which feels like relief... but it may also keep the fear from ever being fully felt, and fading. Remember the students who said worry distracts them from more emotional things? This is what that might look like.

Michelle Newman and Sandra Llera took the idea a step further. Their model is called contrast avoidance. It says that what many people who worry a lot fear most isn't only the bad event. It's the sudden drop... from feeling okay to feeling awful.

In one of their experiments, people worried, relaxed, or thought neutral thoughts... and then watched upsetting film clips. Those who had worried first felt less of a jump when the frightening or sad clip hit. They were already down there. There was less distance to fall.

And here's the part that surprised them. When people with generalized anxiety relaxed first, they were more likely than others to say the sudden switch into the upsetting clip felt hard to bear. Calm, for them, made the drop feel worse.

Think of it like riding with one foot on the brake the whole time, so a sudden stop never jolts you. It works, in a way. But you never get to enjoy the drive. And when nothing bad happens, you've spent the whole evening tense... for nothing.

To be fair, contrast avoidance is a model that's still being tested, mostly in people with generalized anxiety, and mostly in labs. But it explains why worry feels like protection. In a narrow sense... it is.

So is all worry useless? Not quite. In twenty seventeen, Kate Sweeny and Michael Dooley reviewed the research and found real upsides. Moderate worry is linked to people doing protective things... like getting a health screening, or wearing sunscreen.

The difference seems to be where the worry goes. Useful worry ends with something you do. You worry about your skin... you buy the sunscreen... and the thought lets go. Useless worry has no exit. It just circles.

So here are three things researchers have tested. Information, not treatment. First... make it concrete. When a worry starts looping, ask one question. What is the next physical step I could take? If there is one, write it down and give it a time. If there isn't... that's a sign this loop isn't solving anything.

Second... give worry an appointment. This goes back to Borkovec in nineteen eighty-three. Pick a set time and place, say thirty minutes in the early evening. When a worry shows up during the day, jot it down, and postpone it to that slot.

A trial published in twenty twenty-four found that worry dropped in people with generalized anxiety after less than a week of postponing it. But the evidence is mixed. Another study found no clear effect. So treat it as an experiment, not a promise.

Third... keep score. Write the worry down as a prediction, with a date. Then check it later. That's exactly what the students in the Penn State study did. Seeing your own false alarms, in your own handwriting, is hard to argue with.
And if worry is taking over your days, your sleep, or your health, that's not something to fix with a video. Talk to a doctor or a licensed therapist. Worry is very treatable.

So, back to eleven at night. The meeting is tomorrow. Your brain is running the what ifs. Now you know what it's doing. It isn't predicting the future. It's bracing you... keeping you a little bit down, so a fall won't feel so far.
You can thank it for trying. And then ask it one question. What's the next step? If there is one, write it down. If there isn't... the worry can wait for its appointment.
So tell me in the comments. What's one thing you worried about last month that never happened? And if you like your psychology with the receipts, subscribe. There's a new page every week.
